structure: Single-grade Vermont draft framework document (Grade 7 - Vermont and the U.S. from Reconstruction to the Civil Rights Movement). Front matter: header banner, title/theme, Overview narrative, Looking Back/Looking Ahead, Inquiry rationale and contact. Inquiry Process block: 'Inquiry Process (K-12)' statement, a banded list of C3 indicators (6-8) and overarching grade themes. Body is organized by four subject sections (Civics, Economics, Geography, History), each with a 'Theme:' line, C3-strand headings (e.g. Civic and Political Institutions; Economic Decision Making; Geographic Representations; Change, Continuity, and Context) followed by the C3 indicator codes (D2.<Dim>.<n>.6-8). Each strand/indicator group is followed by a 2-column table (R1 headers 'Sample C3 Indicator Connections' | 'Sample Content Connections'; R2 cells hold C1 = 'Students will...' expectations, C2 = bulleted sample content). Rows continued over pages start with 'Continue'. Each subject ends with a 'Resources' list of suggested lessons/inquiries (C3 IDM, iCivics, PBS, etc.). The vermont.gov banner and running headers are furniture. No state-specific standard codes; the D2 C3 codes and the 'Students will' expectations are the standards. Labeling: titles/themes/strand headings/codes/inquiry indicators/'Students will' cells = standards; Sample Content Connections cells, Overview narrative and Resources = examples; Looking Back/Ahead, inquiry rationale, scope notes = backup.
issues: Inquiry Process / C3-indicator / Priority Performance Indicator lists that name a band (K-2, 3-5, 6-8) or K-12 are labeled with that band (shared inquiry skills); everything else is labeled with this file's single grade, per the state guide (one document = one grade).
Resource entries that wrap across pages are split into two units (second unit continues the first); both are labeled examples.
'Note:' lines saying an indicator is not addressed in this grade, and the 'Looking Back/Looking Ahead' paragraphs, are labeled backup.
Civics has only a theme line (u25) and a note (u26) saying Civics C3 indicators are not in grade 7; no civics tables; Global Economy indicators also omitted (note u29).
u40, u57, u111, u117, u174: 'Continue' C1 cells begin or consist of 'Continue' (u40 and u174 also contain 'Students will...' text); labeled standards.
Overarching themes (u21) mention 'Civics - Grades 6 and 8' and 'woven into History'; labeled grade 7 standards.

Grade 7 – Vermont and the U.S. – From Reconstruction to the Civil Rights
Movement (Draft)
Overview

In grade 7, students will build on their knowledge of Vermont and U.S. politics, geography, economics, and peoples as they re-visit the sectional conflicts over slavery that continued into Reconstruction and beyond and led to the long struggle in the 19th and 20th centuries for civil rights. Grade 7 content spans decades; takes students through Reconstruction, industrialization, and world wars, and allows students to dig into critical topics and America’s role in them, such as human rights, the Holocaust, genocide, women’s suffrage, and atomic weaponry. By the end of grade 7, students will have a broad understanding of the roles that politics and power have played both locally and on a world stage; be aware of their changing cultural and physical environments; and gain keen insight as to the ways in which individuals, businesses, governments, and societies make decisions. This broad journey provides a framework for understanding and will allow for deeper analysis of history in high school.
Looking Back

In grade 6, students examined how movement and migration impacted the interactions between expanding civilizations through conquest and trade, including the physical and political geography and ancient societies of Latin America, South and East Asia, Oceania, and Europe.
Looking Ahead

In grade 8, students will utilize past knowledge and understanding to expand their focus on the core concepts and principles underlying America’s democracy. Students will collaborate to identify a problem(s) and develop solutions that would require government involvement and participate in student-led civics projects. Students will also learn about the workings of both national and global economies and develop an understanding of the decision-making processes of individuals, businesses, and governments and how they are connected.
Contact: Martha Deiss, Curriculum & Instruction Division, at Martha.Deiss@vermont.gov
Inquiry

Why inquiry? Using inquiry as an instructional model for the teaching of social studies allows students to authentically ask questions, search for and analyze evidence, and provide explanations and arguments to challenges facing their world.

The inquiry instructional model is driven by authentic questions or problems that have relevance for children. Students learn content, skills, and dispositions as they seek answers to questions and as they apply their learning to take informed action. Pioneered by Dewey (1938), inquiry is an attempt to make classroom experiences feel more like the authentic, curiosity-driven experiences that motivate learning outside of school. (Using Inquiry to Prepare Students for College, Career, and Civic Life, elementary edition, p. 22)

The Inquiry Arc is defined in Dimension 1 (questioning) of the College, Career, and Civic Life (C3) Framework for Social Studies State Standards. In this Framework, Dimension 3 (evidence sourcing), and Dimension 4 (communicating), as well as some evidence indicators found within Dimension 2 – History, have been combined with Dimension 1 into a singular Inquiry Process, as evidenced below. This Inquiry Process begins in the elementary grades and increases in depth and complexity as it spans through high school, preparing students to spiral their learning and skill acquisition in the social studies for college and career readiness.
Inquiry Process (K-12): Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
C3 Indicators (6-8):
Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: D1.1, 2, 3; His. 12
Gathering and Evaluating Sources: D2. His. 6, 10, 12, 13; D3. 1, 2, 3
Communicating and Critiquing Conclusions: D2. His. 16; D4. 1, 2, 4
Overarching Themes:
• Civics – Grades 6 and 8, and woven into History • Disparities and Opportunities • Regional Differences and Migration Patterns • Conflict and Conciliation

Sample Content Connections

Students will be able to explain how industry and trade impact the economy and people of Vermont and the nation. Students will be able to explain how economic systems and policies affected different racial and social groups from Reconstruction to the Modern Civil Rights era.

Individuals and Groups Affected: Indentured servants, enslaved people, Free Blacks, sharecroppers/tenant farmers, women homesteaders, women in the workforce (Rosie the Riveter), entrepreneurs, farmers, mill workers, miners, loggers. Policies/Systems: Black Wall Street, Great Migration, American Indian fur trade, New Deal Programs, farming/agriculture, tourism. Sharecropping and Tenant Farming (Post-Civil War – early 1900s) Economic System: Southern agricultural system where formerly enslaved people and poor white farmers worked land in exchange for a share of the crops. • Effect: African Americans remained in poverty and debt due to unfair contracts; Landowners had more power; limited opportunity for Black economic advancement. Segregated Labor and Low-Wage Jobs (Jim Crow Era) Economic Policy/Practice: Racial segregation in employment; "last hired, first fired." • Effect: African Americans and other minorities often denied skilled jobs, union membership, or fair wages; women, especially women of color, were restricted to low- paying domestic or service jobs. New Deal Programs (1930s) Economic Policy: Government relief programs during the Great Depression (e.g., Social Security, housing assistance, job creation programs). • Effect: Helped many, but excluded farm workers and domestic workers, which affected Black and Latinx workers. Housing programs supported segregation through practices like redlining, denying loans to Black families.

GI Bill After WWII (1944 onward) Economic Policy: Gave returning veterans benefits like college tuition, home loans, and job training. • Effect: White veterans accessed college and bought homes, helping to build middle- class wealth. Black veterans were often denied benefits due to local racism, leaving them economically disadvantaged. Civil Rights Era Economic Focus (1960s) Economic Ideas: “Freedom from poverty” and economic justice became central to the Civil Rights Movement. Examples: Poor People’s Campaign (organized by MLK Jr.) demanded fair wages, jobs, and housing. Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965 aimed to end discrimination, which had long limited economic mobility for Black Americans.

Students will be able to explain the changing role of government in people’s lives over time. Students will be able identify ways the federal government has influenced the economy.

Reconstruction – Gold standard; not much government control over economy or major efforts for tax/spend – Panic of 1873, Panic of 1893; Freedman’s Bureau; land redistribution Progressive Era – Federal Reserve creation, decisions led to 1929 Great Depression; anti- trust laws, Interstate Commerce Commission; Child Labor laws Great Depression – FDR’s New Deal – government spending; jobs programs – WPA, CCC; Social Security; Taxes raised on wealthy; Wagner Act of 1935; Fair Labor Standards Act WWII/post WWII – War production; GI Bill 1960s-1970s – Kennedy tax cuts; Johnson’s Great Society/War on Poverty – fought poverty/boost economy; Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC)

Resources

Fair Labor Practices, Current and Historical- New Jersey: Then and Now - PBS Learning Media: Working conditions in the Paterson silk industry and the farms of the Pinelands varied for the immigrant and seasonal laborers. Labor movements and leaders like Elizabeth Gurley Flynn in Paterson and Elizabeth White at Whitesbog worked to improve the conditions of workers including fair hours, conditions, and benefits. This lesson will examine the labor conditions of historical industries in New Jersey while comparing these with modern fair labor practices and issues both in the country and around the world.

Gilded Age and Progressive Era - Bill of Rights Institute: In these three units - with 8 lessons and 2 videos - students will respond to the following inquiry: “How did Americans at the turn of the 20th century address the rapid technological, demographic, and economic changes around them?” Provide students an in-depth look at this formative period in United States history. Through primary-source-based activities and engaging narratives, students will be exposed to this fascinating period and analyze its numerous parallels to today.

Industrial Revolution: Uncovering America - PBS Learning Media: How did the Industrial Revolution change the United States? What makes industrialization possible? How does art reflect the varying experiences within a capitalist economy? In suggested activities, students consider multiple viewpoints of images from the Industrial Revolution; research and evaluate arguments for and against capitalism; and investigate their own community to create a portrait of their local industry.

The Industrial Age in America: Robber Barons and Captains of Industry - National Endowment for the Humanities: In this lesson students will be able to evaluate the actions taken by various captains of industry and robber barons of the time.

The Industrial Age in America: Sweat Shops. Steel Mills, and Factories - National Endowment for the Humanities: In this lesson, students will analyze the working conditions that led to the Haymarket Affair, the Homestead Strike, and the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire and the actions taken by the managers and workers involved in the incidents, and evaluate the significance of the featured events to the labor movement, the industrialists involved, and the attitude of the American people toward working conditions in the United States.

Human-Environment Interaction: Place, Regions, and Culture
D2.Geo.4.6-8. Explain how cultural patterns and economic decisions influence environments and the daily lives of people in both nearby and distant places.
D2.Geo.6.6-8. Explain how the physical and human characteristics of places and regions are connected to human identities and cultures.
Sample C3 Indicator Connections
Sample Content Connections
Students will be able to explain how geography influenced the culture of the country.

• Enslaved labor was used to transform the Southern landscape for cotton, sugar, and tobacco farming. • Environmental destruction and land exhaustion in the South led to westward expansion. • The South was more rural and dependent on agriculture; the North was more urban and industrial. These differences influenced how Reconstruction played out in each region. • Places in the North and South both had industrializing economies, but at different scales and with different labor systems. • In the South, slavery shaped a distinct human and cultural landscape before the Civil War. • After the war, freed Black communities began building churches, schools, and political organizations—changing the human geography. • Urbanization and migration (especially the Great Migration) moved Black communities into Northern cities, shifting demographics and political power; segregation, Harlem Renaissance.

Students will be able to explain the impact - both intended and unintended - of geographic expansion. Students will be able to explain the impact of westward expansion on Native American communities. Students will be able to explain how immigration and urbanization influenced the country during the post- Reconstruction era.

Geographic Expansion – Louisiana Purchase, Westward Expansion, Annexation of Alaska and Hawaii, Gadsden Purchase, Kansas-Nebraska Act, Annexation of Texas, US Territories, Possession of Philippines Impacts of Expansion – roads, city growth, businesses and industry, railroads, land grants, pollution, ecosystems, loss of native lands, access to natural resources Policies/Acts • Homestead Act (1862) and its long-term effects, Indian Removal policies and the continuation of forced relocations • The Dawes Act (1887) – broke up tribal lands, encouraged assimilation • Reservation system and loss of traditional homelands • Battle of Little Bighorn (1876) and Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) • Boarding schools and the effort to "Americanize" Native children Examples of U.S. Immigration after Reconstruction: Massive immigration after 1870 and how new social patterns, conflicts, and ideas of national unity developed amid growing cultural diversity

Resources

A Cheyenne Odyssey - Mission US: A Public Media Project: Mission US is an award- winning media project that immerses young people in transformational moments in US history; teacher guide. In “A Cheyenne Odyssey,” players become Little Fox, a Northern Cheyenne boy whose life is changed by the encroachment of white settlers, railroads, and U.S. military expeditions. As buffalo diminish and the U.S. expands westward, players experience the Cheyenne’s persistence through conflict and national transformation.

A Cold Reception: Anti-Immigrant Sentiment in the United States - PBS Learning Media: This media-enhanced lesson plan will use video from Dr. Henry Louis Gates Jr.'s PBS series Faces of America to explore the hostile reception immigrants have often received from anti-immigrant "nativists" in an America not always eager to accept them and the change they represent.

A People on the Move- Great Migrations - PBS Learning media: In this lesson, students will contextualize the Great Migration (1910–1940) to better understand its importance and impact on Black Americans and the country. Students will discuss the concepts of resistance and cultural flourishing in the context of the Great Migration. Additionally, students will participate in historical research and presentation, as well as creative expression, to dive deeper into the challenges and triumphs of this historical moment.

City of Immigrants - Mission US: A Public Media Project: Mission US is an award- winning media project that immerses young people in transformational moments in US history; teacher guide. In “City of Immigrants,” players navigate New York’s Lower East Side as Lena, a young Jewish immigrant from Russia. Trying to save money to bring her parents to America, she works long hours in a factory for little money and gets caught up in the growing labor movement.

Hunter-Dunbar Expedition - C3 IDM: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of the Hunter-Dunbar expedition, commissioned by President Thomas Jefferson after the purchase of the Louisiana Territory from France. By investigating the compelling question “Is the Hunter-Dunbar Expedition Worth Remembering?” students evaluate the contributions Dr. George Hunter and William Dunbar made in the discovery and cataloguing of natural resources, geographic features, and Native American groups in the lower portion of the Louisiana Territory (present-day Arkansas). The formative performance tasks build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and help students draw evidence from articles, charts, graphs, and maps while justifying their reasoning in writing.
Grade 7 - The U.S. and Vermont - From Reconstruction to the Civil Rights Movement (Draft) (Revised: November 12, 2025)
Page 15 of 25

Immigration and Displacement: Uncovering America - PBS Learning Media: In this set of artworks and suggested activities, students will explore the motivations of immigration and causes of displacement throughout American history, practice telling stories, investigate transformational journeys, and reflect on the American dream.

Population Profile of Our New Nation: A Comparison of the 1790 and 1800 Censuses - Statistics in Schools: In this activity, students will refer to the 1790 and 1800 censuses to compare the total population with the population of enslaved people, drawing conclusions from the data.

Promised Land - C3 IDM: This inquiry leads students through an investigation of immigration experiences in the United States. By investigating the compelling question “Is America the ‘Promised Land’ for the world’s immigrants?” students evaluate the motivating factors and deterrents for immigration to the United States both in the past and present. The formative performance tasks help students build on knowledge and skills through the course of the inquiry and allow students to recognize the push/pull factors for immigrants throughout our history.

They’re Coming to America: Immigrants Past and Present - PBS Learning Media: In this lesson, students explore the history of this nation of immigrants. In the introductory activity, students identify their own countries of heritage, as well as those of their classmates. Students then identify ethnic groups that migrated to the United States during various historic waves of immigration. In the learning activities, students watch video segments from Faces of America to develop an understanding of key motivations for immigration and explore online resources to examine specific immigrant experiences from various points in American history. In the culminating activity, students utilize their historical knowledge and examination of case studies to develop a brief narrative summarizing the experiences, aspirations, and emotions of a hypothetical immigrant to then the past or the present.

Up from the Dust - Mission US: A Public Media Project: Mission U.S. is an award- winning media project that immerses young people in transformational moments in U.S. history; teacher guide. In “Up from the Dust,” players take on the roles of twins Frank and Ginny Dunn, whose family wheat farm is devastated by the Great Depression and Dust Bowl. As they experience the hardships of the 1930s, players learn about Americans’ strategies for survival – as individuals, communities, and a nation.

After the war, President Wilson promoted the League of Nations (an early idea of global cooperation), though the U.S. didn’t officially join. Example of international negotiation, though it also raised debates about U.S. imperialism. • World War II (1941–1945): The U.S. allied with the United Kingdom, Soviet Union, France, and China to defeat Nazi Germany and Japan. Major example of military and economic cooperation through the Allied Powers. • United Nations (Founded 1945): After WWII, the U.S. helped create the United Nations, a global organization for peace, health, and human rights. The U.S. became a permanent member of the UN Security Council. • Marshall Plan (1948): U.S. gave billions of dollars to help European countries rebuild after WWII. Goal: prevent the spread of communism and support global economic stability.

The American Revolution- PBS Learning Media: This Ken Burns series offers media clips with lessons for grades 6-8: “Demographics of the British Colonies”, Native Americans and British Colonial America: Sovereignty, Diplomacy, and Resistance”, and “Patriot, Loyalist Neutral: Differing Perspectives on the American Revolution”.

African Americans in the Gilded Age - Bill of Rights Institute: Constitutional amendments were ratified during and after the Civil War to protect the natural and civil rights of African Americans. Despite these legal protections, the condition of African Americans significantly worsened in the last few decades of the nineteenth century. An Uphill Battle: Fighting Injustice on the Homefront During WWI - National Archives Harry S. Truman Museum: Students will rotate through four learning centers where they will read primary and secondary sources about injustices during World War I. Civil Rights Movement: The Declaration’s Influence - PBS Learning Media: In this interactive lesson, students explore key speeches given by Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., during the 1960s civil rights movement. They will analyze how he employed language to connect the movement to the Declaration of Independence and to justify its goals.

Fighting for the Right to Fight - The National World War II Museum: This middle school guide provides an introductory essay, profiles of prominent wartime African Americans, and three primary source-based lesson plans.

Korea’s Place in Teaching Social Studies - World History Digital Education.
